paragraphs.heading: What a geologic hazard is
paragraphs.text: A geologic hazard, also called a geohazard, is an adverse geologic condition that can cause widespread damage or loss of property and life. These conditions involve geological processes that may be long-term or short-term. A geohazard can be a relatively small feature. It can also reach huge dimensions, as a submarine or surface landslide can, and it can affect the society and economy of a locality or region to a large extent, as tsunamis do.

paragraphs.heading: How hazards arise
paragraphs.text: Sometimes people set the hazard off. Developments or construction may be carelessly located, without the conditions being taken into account, and activities such as drilling through overpressured zones could bring significant risk. In other cases, particularly in mountain regions, natural processes cause complex events in which one thing triggers another. An avalanche can hit a lake and cause a debris flow, and the consequences may reach hundreds of miles away. Volcanism can create a lahar.

paragraphs.heading: Avoiding the danger
paragraphs.text: A geologic hazard may be avoided by relocation. Publicly available, searchable databases can help people evaluate the hazards at a location they are interested in. Mapping geohazards, by conventional or remote sensing techniques, can also help identify areas suitable for urban development. Planning measures include adopting building codes and regulations that prohibit development near hazard-prone areas.

paragraphs.heading: Building against it
paragraphs.text: Retaining walls can improve the stability of sloping earth, using techniques such as tiebacks, soil nails or soil anchors. On larger projects, gabions and other forms of earth buttress may be used. Revetments and riprap protect shorelines and streams against scour and erosion. The soil or rock itself may be improved by dynamic compaction, by injecting grout or concrete, or with mechanically stabilized earth.

paragraphs.heading: Watching from above
paragraphs.text: In recent decades Earth Observation has become a key tool in managing geohazards, across preparedness, response, recovery and mitigation. It draws on remote sensing technologies, often supported by ground surveys, and supplies critical information to researchers, decision-makers and planners. It has transformed the ability to map and monitor geohazards precisely and promptly.

paragraphs.heading: Volcanism on a global scale
paragraphs.text: Eleven distinct flood basalt episodes took place in the past 250 million years. They resulted in large volcanic provinces and created lava plateaus and mountain ranges. Five mass extinction events have been connected to large igneous provinces. The timing of six of the eleven known provinces coincides with periods of global warming and marine anoxia. This suggests that CO₂ from volcanoes can have an important effect on the climate system.
